title: SQL or NoSQL
idea: SQL databases, such as PostgreSQL, store rows in tables whose columns you declare up front. NoSQL databases, such as MongoDB, keep flexible documents instead.

analogy.text: A spreadsheet and a drawer of index cards. A spreadsheet gives every row the same columns; each card holds whatever you wrote on it.
analogy.breaks: Postgres can hold loose JSON and MongoDB can enforce rules, so the line blurs.

points: A SQL table has a schema: columns and types declared before any row exists.
Postgres rejects a row that breaks the schema, such as a missing required value.
NoSQL is an umbrella term; MongoDB, in chapter 7, stores JSON-like documents.
Tables suit linked records; documents suit self-contained ones.

hero.title: Two ways to store a book

left.title: SQL: PostgreSQL
items: Rows in tables; columns and types are declared first
The database rejects a row that breaks the schema
Related data lives in other tables, linked by ids

right.title: NoSQL: MongoDB
items: Two documents in one collection can differ in shape
Related data can nest inside a document
Rules are optional; your code often enforces the shape

hero.verdict: Neither wins by default: match the database to your data's shape and rules.

code.title: SQL: the schema decides
code.caption: Postgres checks each row against the table. A book with no author is refused, with an error code.

code.title: NoSQL: any shape goes in
code.caption: MongoDB stores whatever shape you send. Two books, two shapes, no error.

pitfalls: Do not choose NoSQL to skip design: your code must then enforce the shape.
Do not assume SQL is rigid: Postgres stores JSON in a `jsonb` column.
Decide from your queries and relations, not from which database is newer.

quiz.why: MongoDB checks no fields by default. Both documents are stored, even though they have different fields.

takeaway: Tables fix the shape up front; documents let each record carry its own.

starters: Can one project use both Postgres and MongoDB?
What does schema mean in a database?
